p10.quote: Product Providers should remain and be ultimately responsible for the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement adopted and record keeping of ownership, regardless of any outsourcing arrangement1.

Product Providers should ensure that proper records of token holders’ ownership interests in the product are maintained and the tokenisation arrangement is operationally compatible with service providers involved2.
For factors of consideration, please also refer to Part A of the Appendix to the Tokenised Securities Circular, where applicable, when formulating the tokenisation arrangement.
the Product Provider should remain fully responsible, despite any outsourcing arrangement such as those envisaged under 6.8 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds.

whether the ownership interest of the underlying assets of the Tokenised Securities are legally valid under the applicable governing laws, whether there are regular reconciliations between the records for the extrinsic rights and the records for the distributed ledger tokens, or whether any encumbrance affects the extrinsic rights.

p14.quote: Product Providers should confirm and, upon SFC’s request, demonstrate to the SFC’s satisfaction the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership and the integrity of the smart contracts5.

5 Product Providers should confirm and demonstrate to the SFC that, at a minimum, they comply with the requirements as set out in paragraphs 10 to 13 above and the smart contracts are not subject to any contract vulnerabilities or security flaws with a high level of confidence.

Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain third party audit or verification on the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership and integrity of the smart contracts.
Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain satisfactory legal opinion to support its application.

gatecoin.quote: Except the Non-Consenting Customers, the 2018 T&C applied to, and governed the relationship between all the Customers (be it Group A, B or C customers) and Gatecoin (Section D2 above). The terms of the 2018 T&C make clear that the cryptocurrencies are not held by Gatecoin on trust for the Customers.

Cryptocurrency is “property” and is capable of being held on trust (Section D4 above). There was certainty of subject matter and object. However, the terms of the 2018 T&C show that there was no certainty of intention to create a trust over the cryptocurrencies held by Gatecoin (Section D5 above).

(vi)The words used by the parties such as ‘trust’, ‘custody’, ‘belonging’, ‘ownership’, ‘title’, may be persuasive, but they are not conclusive in favour of the recognition of B’s proprietary interest in the property, if the terms of the agreement or relationship, viewed objectively, compel a different conclusion.

With the exception of the Non-consenting Customers (“NCCs”), the 2018 T&C applied to, and governed the relationship between all the Customers (be it Group A, B or C) and Gatecoin. Under the 2018 T&C, the Currencies are not held by Gatecoin on trust for the Customers; and
The transactions described in the 7th scenario did not exist and the customers should not be regarded as NCC.

Gatecoin does not hold the Subject Bitcoins or the Specified Account on trust for Mr Samara. The Specified Account is not a NCC and, therefore, Mr Samara is only an unsecured creditor to the extent of his claim less the amount he already received through execution of the HCA Judgment.

The 5th to 7th scenarios prima facie fall outside the definition of NCC but if the customers can prove that they gave the relevant instructions to Gatecoin before the Relevant Date or without using the Platform, they should be regarded as NCCs.

Transactions relating to limit order which a Customer claims was not executed immediately but only when the set price was reached, unless such Customer is able to prove that the order was placed before 6 March 2018.

p10.finding: Paragraph 10 and footnote 1 retain Product Provider responsibility despite outsourcing; paragraph 11 separately requires proper ownership records. These statements do not make a delegation contract, a retained power, a supervision event or a successful outcome a sufficient discharge test. Allocation, exercised conduct, outcomes and their combination remain rival fulfillment proposals. Footnote 1 imports Appendix Part A factors only where applicable. The p10 baseline timed out twice; its tool arm never ran, so no model comparison supports a stronger conclusion.
p10.missing_premises: Governing fulfillment standard, actor/capacity and scheme conditions, effective retained powers, assessed supervision, records and incident chronology within a stated assessment period.
p10.disposition: OPEN_QUALIFIED; source-to-standard and factual application unresolved

p14.finding: Paragraph 14 places 'upon SFC's request' between confirmation and demonstration; footnote 5 specifies minimum objects and a high level of confidence for vulnerabilities/security flaws. The existing A/B/C readings differ over attachment, objects and standards and remain conditional proposals. An absent request can affect the demonstration duty under a request-dependent reading; it does not prove confirmation, underlying compliance or fulfillment. Paragraph 15 audit/verification and paragraph 16 legal opinion have distinct request premises. No numeric confidence threshold follows from footnote 5. Neither live arm ran.
p14.missing_premises: Source argument choosing the attachment/standard, separate request identities and dates, confirmation/demonstration evidence and an applicable substantive assessment standard.
p14.disposition: OPEN_QUALIFIED; preserve rival readings and separate confirmation, demonstration, audit and legal opinion

evidence.finding: A supervision event or completed reconciliation records activity; the retained passages do not make either a sufficient condition for adequate supervision or proper ownership records. Paragraph 11 requires proper records, while Appendix Part A separately raises legal validity, extrinsic rights, encumbrances and reconciliation. A recorded event needs a governing sufficiency standard and scoped facts before it can support that normative judgment. Source text retrieval and CAES labels supplied with artificial weights add no such warrant. Neither live arm ran.
evidence.missing_premises: Applicable adequacy/propriety standard, completeness and quality of the activity, discrepancies and remediation, legal title/rights, actor identity, coverage of the assessment interval and contrary observations.
evidence.disposition: OPEN_QUALIFIED; activity-to-adequacy inference remains unsupported without these premises

gatecoin.finding: The 2023 conclusion distinguishes cryptocurrency's capacity to be trust property from an actual trust under the operative terms, preserving the non-consenting-customer exception. Terms and objective relationships matter; labels and agency alone are not conclusive. The 2025 decision carries forward that finding and distinguishes customer consent, pooled beneficial interests, ETD claims and the separate Samara relationship. Paragraph 8 treats scenario seven as absent, paragraph 95 groups five to seven in its exception wording, and the annexure gives its own categories. This tension remains unresolved. These exchange-insolvency decisions supply factors to investigate, not a universal 26EC22 fulfillment test. Neither live arm ran.
gatecoin.missing_premises: Specific target actors and rights, governing law and operative terms, acceptance/consent evidence, analogous facts and a warranted legal transfer; complete later treatment and reconciliation of the scenario-seven passages.
gatecoin.disposition: OPEN_QUALIFIED; no current-treatment certification or automatic target classifier
